newsitem.title: USA: U.S. industry pace slows as growth moderates.
newsitem.headline: U.S. industry pace slows as growth moderates.

text.p: Factories were less busy as summer ended last month, a closely watched industry survey confirmed Tuesday, as a key forecasting gauge predicted slower but steady economic growth through year-end.

The two reports -- from the National Association of Purchasing Management and the private Conference Board -- sketched out a picture of a slowing national economy that apparently persuaded Federal Reserve policy-makers against boosting interest rates a week ago.

Most analysts have forecast that the expansion eased in the third quarter that ended Monday to around a 2.5 percent annual rate from the second quarter's hot 4.7 percent pace that had fired up inflation fears.
The NAPM said its index of manufacturing activity fell to 51.7 last month from 52.6 in August, indicating growth in September was at a slower rate than in August.
A reading above 50 points to growth in manufacturing, while one below that level signals contraction.
The NAPM reading reassured markets that the economy has lost some momentum after growing at the most vigorous pace in two years during the spring.
The 30-year Treasury jumped 21/32, or $6.56 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 6.87 percent from 6.92 percent on Monday.

The Conference Board's Index of Leading Indicators posted a seventh straight monthly rise in August, up a modest 0.2 percent after an identical July rise. It is supposed to predict economic trends six to nine months ahead, and analysts said its performance was consistent with steady but more muted growth.
The NAPM index, which measures not only orders and backlogs but price changes, is well-regarded by private forecasters and by the central bank as a broad-based indicator of inflation trends.
Federal Reserve policymakers met Sept. 24 and left interest rates steady, evidently anticipating the economy was slowing enough on its own to contain wage and price inflation.

The NAPM said its index of prices paid by manufacturers rose in September for the first time in four months. But faster deliveries from suppliers, which mean less inflationary bottlenecks during production, and weakness in the employment and inventory readings muted inflation worries.
"The report shows the manufacturing sector is just muddling through," said Elliott Platt, research director at Donaldson Lufkin and Jenrette in New York.
Ralph Kauffman, chairman of NAPM's business survey committee, similarly foresaw neither a dramatic slowing nor a pickup on the horizon.
"I think continued steady growth at approximately the level we've seen recently is probably indicated for the very near term," Kauffman said.
The Conference Board's leading index suggested the same -- rising national output this fall and winter but at a more subdued pace than in the spring.

The leading index measures a basket of economic indicators, from unemployment benefit claims to building permits. Seven of its 11 components were stronger in August, while four showed some weakening from July.
Economist Daryl Delano of Cahners Economics Inc. in Newton, Mass., said the leading index showed the economy "was moving along pretty well" in the third quarter.
"But given two straight months of very small increases, this plays into the general thinking that later this year and early in 1997 the economy is certainly going to be slowing," Delano said.

The signals of rising activity in August were led by increased commodity prices, higher stock prices and fewer new claims for unemployment pay. In addition, vendor delivery times slowed because companies were busier, the average workweek lengthened, the money supply increased and consumer expectations strengthened.

The negative indicators were paced by a decline in order backlogs and by fewer new orders for plant and equipment. Consumer goods orders also fell from July and there were fewer applications for building permits.
Separately Tuesday, the research firm BTM/Schroders said its latest survey of chain stores showed sales fell 1.2 percent in the week ended Sept. 28 from the prior week.
"The latest week's sales were generally below plan for most retailers with the discount segment of the business particularly weak," BTM/Schroders said.
Consumers, burdened by debt, are thought to have curbed spending in the third quarter. Sales by retail stores advanced only fractionally in July and August, the government previously reported.
